description_full: Kinross Gold Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the acquisition, exploration, and development of gold properties principally in the United States, Brazil, Chile, Canada, and Mauritania. It is also involved in the extraction and processing of gold-containing ores; reclamation of gold mining properties; and production and sale of silver. The company was founded in 1993 and is headquartered in Toronto, Canada.

financial_summary: Kinross Gold Corporation is a large-cap basic materials business with a $24.5B market cap on $7.1B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +27% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +5.7pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 32%.

The business throws off $2.6B in free cash flow — roughly 36 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.52× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 25× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 3.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 3.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Weakness in commodity prices pressures materials companies
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sect: Its 46% operating margin runs 37pp above the Basic Materials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 3.57x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.4% of sector revenue and 1.5% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+1.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 221 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 8% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 47% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 55% and a beta of 0.91, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.49 vs 5y 0.84), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $189.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 42% in the 2020 crash, 50% in the 2022 bear market and 71% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 26% below its DCF fair value of $28.22, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 63%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $21.59 to $37.62 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Basic Materials peers: P/E 7.9 vs 16.3, EV/EBITDA 4.2 vs 8.3 and P/FCF 9.5 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 26% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 10.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 14.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 10 covering analysts target $30.68 on average, 48% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.2%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.99).
It runs a 32% gross margin and converts 36% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 9/9 and cash conversion of 1.52x.
ROE of 29% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 23pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $1.0B.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.9, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 26.8% over 3 years and 10.8% over 5 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 16%).
At current returns, reinvesting 36% of profits supports about 2.1% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 19.8% a year over five years.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 8.9% on average.
Analysts expect 8.6% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 70%.
It returns 3.1% a year to shareholders (2.5% in buybacks and 0.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: CEO pay is $3.8M, and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
